britannica-1911-bashi-bazouk:
Bashi-bazouk was the name for a kind of irregular mounted troops employed by the Turks, as explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The government armed and maintained them, but they received no pay. They wore no uniform and no distinctive badges, and they fought either on horseback or on foot, chiefly on foot. Lack of discipline, the entry says, made them incapable of serious work in battle, despite their numbers and their rough readiness to fight.

Usefulness and abuse stand side by side in the account. Bashi-bazouks often served well in reconnaissance, riding ahead to scout, and in outpost duty. Yet the entry accuses them, generally with justice, of robbing and mistreating civilians, and says Turkish regular troops sometimes had to disarm them by force. The name also covered a peacetime mounted force in Turkish provinces that did the work of gendarmerie, or rural police.
britannica-1911-beothuk:
Beothuk were a tribe of North American Indians who once lived in the interior of Newfoundland. A mystery hangs over them, because the few words of their language that survive point to a stock distinct from their neighbours. Their name, of Micmac origin, is said to mean simply “red men.”

The Beothuk stood in bitter hostility to the French settlers of the island. They were hunted down and killed off over the years, until in 1820 a few survivors escaped into Labrador. The last of the tribe is believed to have died in 1829. The entry is brief, and its brevity itself tells the story: a whole people gone, leaving only a name and a handful of words.
britannica-1911-habakkuk:
Habakkuk is the eighth book of the Old Testament Minor Prophets. The name appears twice inside the book itself. It appears nowhere else in the Old Testament. Its meaning is uncertain. It may come from a Hebrew root meaning to embrace. Scholars link it more plausibly to an Assyrian plant name. Of the man himself almost nothing is known. Legends attach to him, including Bel and the Dragon. Those tales carry no historic value.

Most of the long article is critical argument. Scholars dispute how the book's parts fit together. The prophet complains of wickedness and injustice. God answers by raising up the Chaldaeans. Later passages denounce Chaldaean tyranny in detail. Giesebrecht, Budde, Davidson and Driver all rearrange the text differently. Each theory moves chapter one passages to new places. Dating proposals run from before 597 BC onward. Duhm even placed the whole book near Alexander's time.
britannica-1911-huber-johann-nepomuk:
Johann Nepomuk Huber (1830–1879) was a German philosophical and theological writer, a leader of the Old Catholics, born at Munich on the 18th of August 1830. Meant for the priesthood, he began with theology. The writings of Spinoza and Oken drew him strongly to philosophy, and in philosophy he qualified at Munich's university in 1854. He became professor there in time, extraordinary in 1859 and ordinary in 1864.

With Döllinger and others, Huber drew wide public notice in 1869. Their treatise Der Papst und das Koncil, signed with the pen name Janus, challenged the Ultramontane promoters of the Vatican council. In 1870 came the Römische Briefe, letters recast from secret reports sent from Rome during the council's sitting. The account follows his part in the Old Catholic movement that rose when the council defined papal infallibility, and the books in which he set out its case against Rome.
britannica-1911-keokuk:
Keokuk is a city of Lee county, Iowa, on the Mississippi river at the mouth of the Des Moines, in the southeast corner of the state, about 200 miles above St Louis. Its people numbered 14,641 in 1900 and 14,008 in 1910. Four railways serve it, and bridges of about 2200 feet and 1200 feet cross the Mississippi and the Des Moines.

The city has a public library, two hospitals, and the Keokuk Medical College, founded in 1849, and a national cemetery lies there. Much of the city is built on bluffs along the Mississippi. Keokuk stands at the foot of the Des Moines Rapids. Round the rapids the federal government has built a ship canal, opened in 1877, about 9 miles long, and at its foot a great dam. The entry gives the town the full civic treatment of its age, from its bluffs and bridges to its trade on the river.
britannica-1911-kerkuk:
Kerkuk is the chief town of a sanjak in the Mosul vilayet of Asiatic Turkey. It stands among the foothills of the Kurdistan Mountains at about 1100 feet, on both banks of the Khassa Chai, a tributary of the Tigris. Its people are put at 12,000 to 15,000, mostly Muslim Kurds.

Set where several routes meet, the town has a brisk transit trade in hides, Persian silks and cottons, dyestuffs, fruit, and timber. Its chief weight, though, comes from its petroleum and naphtha springs. Warm springs near by supply baths and are said to have healing powers. In the neighbourhood is a burning mountain, known locally for many centuries. Kerkuk is clearly an old site: its citadel stands on an artificial mound 130 feet high. It was a metropolitan see of the Chaldean Christians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-habacuc-habak:
Habakkuk, eighth of the Minor Prophets, probably flourished near the end of the seventh century before Christ, though the entry admits almost nothing certain about his life. His Hebrew name, an intensive form often read as embrace, survives differently in the Septuagint and Vulgate. Legends make him a Levite, a son of the Shunammite woman, or the prophet who fed Daniel, none of it reliable.

His short book divides into a dialogue with God over Judah's wrongs and the coming Chaldeans, with five woes against the conqueror, and a lyric prayer describing God's saving appearance. Scholars dispute its date, from Manasseh's last years to Josiah, Jehoiakim, or the Exile itself. The entry weighs each view against the book's own references to events before the Babylonian captivity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kerkuk:
Kerkuk, ancient Karka of Beit-Slokh, is a Chaldean Catholic diocese in the Mosul region, on the borderlands of the old Persian Empire. This entry sketches a Christian community that goes back to martyrs of 318 and metropolitans who sat at councils between 410 and 612.

Bishops and saints fill the early record, from fourth-century Mana and his six nuns to St. Sirina in 559. After Nestorians accepted papal authority in the early nineteenth century, the pope set up the present diocese. It counts 6,000 Catholics, 15 stations, 16 churches and chapels, 22 native priests, and five primary schools. Kerkuk town itself, with 30,000 people, holds only some 300 or 400 Catholics, the rest being Muslims, Jews, or Nestorians.
podcast-dannyjones-TGbtz6L3quk:
Comedian Kurt Metzger joins Danny Jones for the episode built around his scorched-earth verdict on America, delivered in the title's furious quote about what the powerful do to children. Metzger, a writer known for refusing every party line, uses the hour to accuse elites across politics and entertainment in the language of a man done being careful.

Jones mostly winds him up and points him at topics: Epstein, media, war, and the entertainment industry that employed them both. Metzger's charges are rhetoric and allegation mixed, offered as comedy's license and a citizen's rage at once; nothing here is a documented finding. The episode's value is tonal. It preserves the sound of a certain American fury in 2020s podcast form, profane, funny, and sincerely convinced the country is run by monsters.
podcast-joerogan-0Z9wmqlypUk:
Lorenzo Hagerty joins Joe Rogan for episode 419 of the Joe Rogan Experience, in its second part. Hagerty is the psychedelic archivist known as the man behind a vast trove of drug lore talks. Fans call him a wise elder of the scene.

Hagerty and Rogan roam the lore of plant drugs, from old rites to new labs. He shares tales of the minds he taped and the trips that taught him most. Rogan hears him as a link to a lost age of the scene. Listeners get a deep cut for lore fans. The library keeps the episode as a record of the return visit.
tanakh-jps-1917-habakkuk:
Habakkuk is one of the short prophetic books, here in the Jewish Publication Society rendering of the Holy Scriptures from 1917. Little is told of the man; the book is called the burden that Habakkuk the prophet saw.

The prophet cries out at the wrong and strife he sees around him, asking how long God will watch and not save. He charges that law has gone slack and right is twisted, since the wicked hem in the just. Readers meet a bold talk with God about pain and delay, brief in length yet deep in trust, ending in praise sung when all earthly props have failed.
